title: Writing a workflow
bridge: An activity call in a workflow is like an API call inside a React component. Except: Temporal retries it for you, so the activity must be safe to run twice. And its result is recorded, so a replay never calls it again.
intro: This lesson writes workflow code the way the platform does: deterministic, with every outside call behind proxyActivities. You set the two timeouts Nova uses and learn why 7 days is never a work limit. Then you watch a heartbeat bring a killed activity back.

picture.caption: The activity heartbeats while it follows the VM. If its worker dies, Temporal retries, and the new attempt re-attaches to the same VM.

p: A workflow must make the same calls in the same order every time it is replayed. So workflow code has no I/O: no fetch, no files, no Node modules. The worker enforces part of this, because it bundles workflows without Node's built-in modules.

Time and randomness are handled for you. Inside a workflow, Date.now() returns the time of the current step, not the real clock, and Math.random() is seeded. They give the same answer on replay. Still, the tickets say no Date.now() for logic: use sleep() and condition() timeouts for anything about time. condition() waits until something becomes true, with an optional timeout (p7-3).
Use workflowInfo() for facts about the run, such as runId and historyLength. Everything else comes in as arguments or as activity results.

p: proxyActivities gives the workflow stand-ins for your activities, with options. The SDK requires a timeout. startToCloseTimeout is the longest one attempt may run. heartbeatTimeout is the longest gap allowed between two heartbeats of a running attempt.
G3-29 keeps the options in one file, policies.ts, with two presets. SHORT is 5 minutes, for calls to Jira, Slack and AWS. LONG is 7 days with 2-minute heartbeats, for anything that follows a VM.
sections.because: We keep timeouts in one presets file because every workflow should treat a slow call the same way.

notes.text: Workflow-side imports only. ActivityOptions and RetryPolicy are the option types.
Type-only import of every activity, so the stand-ins are typed and the activity code stays out of the bundle.
SHORT: one attempt may take 5 minutes. A Jira call that hangs longer is cut and retried.
The comment from the ticket. Read it twice: this timeout never limits the agent's work.
LONG: a far safety net plus a 2-minute heartbeat. The heartbeat, not the 7 days, catches a dead worker.

sections.h: Retry policies: how often, and when to stop
p: When an attempt fails, Temporal waits and tries again. A RetryPolicy says how: the first wait, how fast the wait grows, the longest wait, and how many attempts. A wait that grows after each failure is called back-off. maximumAttempts 0, or no value, means no limit.

Some errors must never be retried. An activity marks one with ApplicationFailure.create({ type, nonRetryable: true }), or the policy lists the type in nonRetryableErrorTypes. A person who pressed Stop is StoppedByPerson: retrying it would ignore that person.
sections.because: We pick a policy per kind of call because AWS throttling, a Jira outage and a refused scope need different answers.

notes.text: Errors that are decisions, not glitches. Retrying them would undo a person's choice or a wall.
AWS: 1 s, 2 s, 4 s ... up to 1 minute between tries.
At most 10 tries for AWS; then the error reaches the workflow.
Jira, Slack and GitHub: no attempt limit. A long outage pauses the ticket instead (G3-39).
Check with G3-29's owner where this is used: a workInSandbox with one attempt could not re-attach (next sections).
act: the default proxy, LONG with AWS retries. Workflows call act.acquireSandbox, act.workInSandbox and so on.
peopleApis: short calls to people's tools, retried with back-off and no limit.

p: A long activity calls heartbeat() from @temporalio/activity now and then. Each call tells the service: this attempt is alive. You can pass details, such as how far you got.

If the heartbeats stop for longer than heartbeatTimeout, the service ends the attempt and schedules a new one. The new attempt can read the last details with activityInfo().heartbeatDetails and continue from there. That is the code you run in the lab.
sections.because: We heartbeat so a dead worker shows up in 2 minutes, not after 7 days.

notes.text: Activity-side helpers. heartbeat and activityInfo work only inside a running activity.
On attempt 1 there are no details, so done is 0. On a retry it is the last step a dead attempt reported.
attempt counts from 1. You will see this line after you kill the worker.
Heartbeats are throttled by the SDK, so calling it often is fine; it sends at most one every few seconds.

sections.h: 7 days is a safety net, not a work limit
p: Nova's agent may work for hours. No time, turn or budget limit may cut it off; that is a wall of the platform. So why does workInSandbox have a 7-day timeout at all? Because the SDK requires one.

The trick is that workInSandbox only follows the agent; the agent runs on the VM under systemd. If an attempt ends, from a dead worker or the 7 days, Temporal retries. The new attempt sees the harness already running and follows it again. The agent never notices.

A dead VM is different. The harness heartbeat stops, and after 5 minutes workInSandbox throws SandboxDead, marked non-retryable. The workflow catches it and recovery takes a fresh VM from the last checkpoint (G3-27). A checkpoint is the harness saving its work: it pushes the branch and saves the session.
sections.because: We start the harness only when it is not running; that check makes a retry re-attach instead of starting a second agent.

notes.text: Idempotent start: attempt 2 finds the systemd unit from attempt 1 and does not start another agent.
The harness heartbeat comes from a timer in nova-worker, not the model loop, so slow thinking never looks dead.
The activity returns when the agent stops for a reason: done, a question, a Spot warning or a failure.
No harness heartbeat for 5 minutes: the VM is gone. Not retried here; the workflow's recovery decides.
The activity's own heartbeat to Temporal. The checkpoint sha rides along, so the workflow knows the latest one.
A plain timer is fine here: this is activity code, not workflow code.

callout.text: No maxTurns, no maxBudgetUsd, no taskBudget, no time limit on an agent. Timeouts in Temporal only detect dead machines.

p: Every VM a run claims must be released, whatever happens: success, failure, or a person pressing Stop. A try/finally does that. One detail: Stop cancels the workflow, and a cancelled workflow cannot start new activities.
CancellationScope.nonCancellable runs its function even while the run is being cancelled. So releaseSandbox still runs. The activities are idempotent: release accepts a VM that is already gone.
sections.because: We release in finally inside nonCancellable because a cancelled run must still free its VM.

notes.text: runId from workflowInfo(): deterministic, and unique for this run.
The long call with LONG options. It returns when the agent is done or needs an answer.
finally runs on success, on an error and on cancellation.
nonCancellable: the release runs even when Stop cancelled the run.

sections.h: Errors that come back to the workflow
p: When an activity gives up, the workflow's await throws an ActivityFailure. Its cause holds the real error. For our own errors that is an ApplicationFailure with a type, such as SandboxDead or LabNotReady.

Recovery (G3-27) checks err instanceof ActivityFailure && err.cause instanceof ApplicationFailure and reads err.cause.type. Every other error is thrown again and fails the run. Match on the type string, never on the message text.

callout.text: An activity is idempotent when running it twice has the same effect as once. claim finds its own VM by tag, release accepts a VM that is already gone. Write every activity this way.

quiz.q: workInSandbox reaches its 7-day startToCloseTimeout while the agent is still working. What happens?

options.text: The agent on the VM is stopped and the work is lost
options.why: Temporal never touches the VM; only the attempt that follows the agent ends.

options.text: The workflow fails with a timeout error
options.why: With retries allowed, a timed-out attempt is retried, not reported as a failure.

options.text: The attempt ends, Temporal retries, and the new attempt finds the harness running and follows it
options.why: That is re-attach: the timeout is a safety net, never a work limit.

quiz.q: Which error type belongs in nonRetryableErrorTypes?

options.why: A person's decision must not be retried; it is in NEVER_RETRY.
Throttling is a glitch; back-off retries are exactly the answer.
A dropped connection should be retried with back-off by PEOPLE_APIS.

quiz.q: Why is releaseSandbox called inside CancellationScope.nonCancellable in finally?

options.why: It changes when the call may run, not how fast it is.

options.text: So a run that a person stopped still frees its VM
options.why: Stop cancels the workflow; without nonCancellable the release activity would not start.

options.text: So the release is retried forever
options.why: Retries come from the retry policy, not from the scope.

tickets.why: policies.ts is the presets and retry policies from this lesson, in one file every workflow imports.
workInSandbox starts the harness once and follows its heartbeat, which makes a retry re-attach.
ticketToPr's inSandbox uses try/finally with nonCancellable so every VM is released.
Recovery catches ActivityFailure whose cause is an ApplicationFailure of type SandboxDead.

remember: Workflow code only decides. Activities do the work, heartbeat, and are safe to retry, so a timeout re-attaches instead of cutting work off.
